title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
tagline: Why atoms bond, how the shape of a molecule follows from its electron pairs, and what holds molecules to each other.

overview.intro: Chemical bonding explains why sodium and chlorine react explosively while neon never reacts at all, why water is bent rather than linear, and why ammonia smells but neon does not. This unit begins with the Kossel-Lewis approach and the octet rule, follows the complete transfer of electrons that gives an ionic bond and the electron sharing that gives a covalent one, and then turns to the three modern theories that predict molecular geometry and polarity: VSEPR for shape, valence bond theory with hybridisation for orbital overlap, and molecular orbital theory for magnetic and bonding behaviour that valence bond theory cannot explain. Hydrogen bonding closes the unit by showing how an unusually strong intermolecular attraction changes the physical properties of a substance.

learningOutcomes: Apply the Kossel-Lewis approach to draw Lewis structures, assign formal charges and predict the stability of species.
Describe ionic bond formation, lattice energy and the covalent character introduced by Fajans' rules.
Use VSEPR to predict molecular geometry and use bond parameters and dipole moments to compare molecules.
Use valence bond theory, hybridisation and molecular orbital theory to explain bonding, shape and magnetism, and distinguish the two types of hydrogen bonding.

learn.title: The Kossel-Lewis approach and the ionic bond

blocks.text: Kossel observed that noble gases have stable electronic configurations — eight valence electrons except helium's two — and that atoms react either by losing electrons to reach the configuration of the preceding noble gas or by gaining electrons to reach that of the following one. Lewis added that the shared pair in a covalent bond lets both atoms complete their octet. The approach works for most of the periodic table: sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to become Na⁺ with the neon configuration, chlorine (2,8,7) gains one to become Cl⁻ with the argon configuration, and the electrostatic attraction between the resulting oppositely charged ions is the electrovalent or ionic bond.

Ionic compounds exist as giant three-dimensional lattices in which each cation is surrounded by an equal number of anions and vice versa; the formula NaCl is a ratio, not a molecule. Forming gaseous ions from the elements requires energy — ionisation enthalpy of the metal plus electron gain enthalpy of the non-metal — and is often endothermic, but the enormous lattice energy released when the ions come together in the crystal makes the overall process favourable. Lattice energy rises with the charges of the ions and falls with their size, so magnesium oxide (Mg²⁺O²⁻) has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride. Because a small, highly charged cation polarises the electron cloud of a large anion, some seemingly ionic compounds acquire appreciable covalent character: aluminium chloride and beryllium chloride are molecular solids rather than typical ionic lattices, a consequence described by Fajans' rules.

Bond polarity arises when the shared pair is drawn closer to one atom. Electronegativity difference decides how unequal the sharing is: a difference above about 1.7 gives predominantly ionic bonding, between roughly 0.4 and 1.7 gives a polar covalent bond, and below 0.4 is essentially non-polar covalent. The dipole moment μ = q × d (in debye, where 1 D = 3.33564 × 10⁻³⁰ C m) measures the polarity of a whole molecule, and because it is a vector, symmetrical molecules such as CO₂ and BF₃ have zero dipole moment even though their individual bonds are polar, while the bent H₂O and pyramidal NH₃ have substantial moments.

items.meaning: The tendency of atoms to achieve eight valence electrons, as in the nearest noble gas.
The energy released when gaseous ions combine to form one mole of an ionic crystal.
The product of the separated charge and the distance between them, μ = q × d, measured in debye.

learn.title: Bond parameters and the VSEPR theory

blocks.text: Bond parameters quantify a bond: bond length is the equilibrium distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms, decreasing with bond order (C–C 154 pm, C=C 134 pm, C≡C 120 pm); bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of a bond homolytically in the gaseous state; bond angle is the angle between two bonds meeting at a central atom; and bond order — the number of shared pairs — predicts both length and strength. Ionic bonds have no discrete molecules, so their "length" is the interionic distance in the lattice, while covalent and coordinate (dative) bonds, in which both electrons of the shared pair come from one atom as in NH₄⁺, do have discrete lengths and energies.

VSEPR theory predicts shape from the repulsion between electron pairs around a central atom. The pairs — bonding and lone — arrange themselves as far apart as possible, and the repulsions follow the order lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bonding pair > bonding pair-bonding pair. This gives the familiar sequence: two electron domains are linear (180°), three are trigonal planar (120°), four are tetrahedral (109.5°), five are trigonal bipyramidal and six are octahedral. Lone pairs then compress the ideal angles because they occupy more space: CH₄ stays at 109.5°, NH₃ with one lone pair closes to 107°, and H₂O with two lone pairs closes to 104.5°. Repulsion between lone pairs on the same atom also explains why the lone pairs of SF₄ occupy the equatorial positions of the trigonal bipyramid.

Multiple bonds count as one domain but repel more strongly, slightly reducing adjacent angles (H₂C=O shows ~120° compressed).

A coordinate bond is indistinguishable from an ordinary covalent bond once formed, as in the four equivalent N–H bonds of NH₄⁺.

blocks.text: Valence bond theory explains a covalent bond as the overlap of two half-filled atomic orbitals, one from each atom, whose electron spins pair up. The greater the effective overlap, the stronger the bond, so head-on overlap along the internuclear axis gives a strong sigma (σ) bond while side-on overlap above and below that axis gives a weaker pi (π) bond. A single bond is always σ; a double bond is one σ plus one π; a triple bond is one σ plus two π. Because only orbitals of comparable energy and direction overlap well, a carbon atom that is to form four equivalent bonds does not use one 2s and three 2p orbitals of very different shape — it promotes an electron and hybridises them.

Hybridisation is the mixing of atomic orbitals on the same atom to give an equal number of new hybrid orbitals directed to give the minimum repulsion. sp hybridisation mixes one s and one p to give two linear orbitals at 180° (BeCl₂, ethyne, HCN); sp² mixes one s and two p to give three trigonal planar orbitals at 120° (BF₃, ethene, formaldehyde); sp³ mixes one s and three p to give four tetrahedral orbitals at 109.5° (CH₄, NH₃, H₂O). sp³d and sp³d² hybridisation, invoking the d orbitals of the third period, give the trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅) and octahedral (SF₆) shapes. The shape of a molecule follows the hybridisation of its central atom, and the number of σ bonds plus lone pairs on that atom tells you which hybrid set is present.

items.text: State the hybridisation and shape of the carbonate ion CO₃²⁻.
items.note: The central carbon has three bonding domains and no lone pairs, so it is sp² hybridised and the ion is trigonal planar with bond angles of 120°; one of the three C=O descriptions is a resonance form, so all three C–O bonds are equivalent at 128 pm.

items.text: How many σ and π bonds are present in ethyne, HC≡CH?
items.note: Each C–H bond is a σ bond formed by overlap of C sp with H 1s, giving two σ bonds, and the C≡C triple bond consists of one σ bond plus two π bonds formed by side-on overlap of the remaining unhybridised p orbitals. Total: 3 σ and 2 π bonds.

blocks.text: Molecular orbital theory goes further by treating electrons as delocalised over the whole molecule. When two atomic orbitals combine they form two molecular orbitals: a bonding MO of lower energy, with increased electron density between the nuclei, and an antibonding MO of higher energy, marked with an asterisk and having a node between the nuclei. The order of filling for homonuclear diatomics up to N₂ is σ1s, σ*1s, σ2s, σ*2s, σ2pz, then π2px = π2py, then their antibonding partners; from O₂ onward the σ2pz lies below the π set. Bond order = (number of bonding electrons − number of antibonding electrons)/2, so O₂ with 10 bonding and 6 antibonding electrons has a bond order of 2, while O₂⁺ has 2.5 and O₂⁻ has 1.5 — a sequence that correctly predicts the shortening and lengthening observed experimentally.

learn.title: Molecular orbitals of homonuclear diatomics and hydrogen bonding

blocks.text: The most striking success of MO theory is the magnetic behaviour of oxygen. Each O atom contributes six 2p electrons, giving twelve valence electrons; filling the molecular orbitals in the order σ2pz, π2px = π2py, π*2px = π*2py leaves the last two electrons unpaired in the two degenerate π* orbitals, following Hund's rule. Liquid oxygen is therefore paramagnetic and is attracted to a magnetic field, a fact the Lewis structure, with its paired electrons, cannot explain. Nitrogen, with ten valence electrons and a fully filled bonding set, is diamagnetic with a bond order of 3, and the loss of one electron to form N₂⁺ lowers its bond order to 2.5 and lengthens the bond.

Hydrogen bonding is the strong attraction between a hydrogen atom already bonded to a highly electronegative atom (N, O or F) and a lone pair on a neighbouring N, O or F atom. The polar X–H bond leaves hydrogen almost as a bare proton, and the electrostatic attraction to the lone pair is much stronger than an ordinary dipole interaction. It may be intramolecular, as in o-nitrophenol where the hydrogen bonds within the molecule, or intermolecular, as in water, where a network of hydrogen bonds gives a boiling point of 100 °C compared with the 60 °C expected from hydrogen sulphide's trend. Hydrogen bonding raises boiling points, increases viscosity and surface tension, and is the reason ice is less dense than liquid water: in ice each oxygen is tetrahedrally hydrogen-bonded to four neighbours, holding the molecules apart in an open lattice.

items.text: Calculate the bond order of the superoxide ion O₂⁻ and comment on its bond length.
items.note: O₂⁻ has 17 electrons in total: 10 bonding (σ1s, σ*1s, σ2s, σ*2s, σ2pz and the π2px, π2py pair) and 7 antibonding. Bond order = (10 − 7)/2 = 1.5, so the O–O bond is weaker and longer than the double bond of O₂ (order 2, 121 pm) and longer than that of O₂⁺ (order 2.5, 112 pm); the superoxide bond is about 133 pm.

items.text: Explain why hydrogen fluoride is associated as H₂F₂ in the vapour phase.
items.note: Each HF molecule has a highly polar H–F bond and three lone pairs on fluorine. The partially positive hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to a lone pair of fluorine on another, forming a zig-zag (HF)ₙ chain; in the vapour at moderate pressures the simplest associate is the dimer H₂F₂, with F–H⋯F close to linear. The hydrogen bond raises the boiling point of HF well above that of the heavier hydrogen halides.

keyPoints: Atoms bond to reach a stable octet (duet for hydrogen); electrons are transferred (ionic) or shared (covalent).
Ionic compounds are giant lattices; lattice energy rises with ionic charge and falls with ionic size.
Fajans' rules: a small, highly polarising cation with a large polarisable anion gives covalent character.
Bond polarity depends on electronegativity difference; molecular polarity is the vector sum of bond dipoles.
VSEPR: domains minimise repulsion; lone pairs compress angles (CH₄ 109.5°, NH₃ 107°, H₂O 104.5°).
Valence bond theory: σ bonds from head-on overlap, π bonds from side-on overlap; double = 1σ + 1π.
Hybridisation: sp linear, sp² trigonal planar, sp³ tetrahedral, sp³d trigonal bipyramidal, sp³d² octahedral.
Bond order = (bonding − antibonding electrons)/2; O₂ has bond order 2 and two unpaired electrons.
Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on a neighbouring N, O or F.
Hydrogen bonds raise boiling points and make ice less dense than liquid water.
examFocus: Drawing Lewis structures, assigning formal charge and stating shape and hybridisation is the classic 2-3 mark sequence in this 7-mark unit.
Explain the water-ammonia-methane angle sequence with lone-pair repulsion; it is the standard analytical answer.
Compute bond order from MO configurations and use it to compare bond lengths and magnetism of O₂, O₂⁺ and O₂⁻.

vocabulary.meaning: The bond formed by the complete transfer of one or more electrons from one atom to another.
A covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair come from the same atom.
The mixing of atomic orbitals on one atom to give an equal number of equivalent hybrid orbitals.
A bond formed by head-on overlap of orbitals along the internuclear axis.
A bond formed by side-on overlap of p orbitals above and below the internuclear axis.
A molecular orbital of higher energy with a node between the nuclei that weakens bonding.
An electrostatic attraction between hydrogen bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on a neighbouring N, O or F atom.

questions.prompt: The shape of the ammonia molecule NH₃ is:
questions.explanation: Nitrogen has four electron domains — three bonding pairs and one lone pair — giving a tetrahedral electron geometry, but the molecular shape counts only the atoms: one lone pair compresses the trigonal arrangement into a trigonal pyramid with a bond angle of 107°.

questions.prompt: The bond order of the O₂ molecule according to molecular orbital theory is:
questions.explanation: O₂ has 16 electrons; filling the molecular orbitals gives 10 bonding and 6 antibonding electrons, so bond order = (10 − 6)/2 = 2. The two remaining electrons occupy separate π* orbitals with parallel spins, which is why oxygen is paramagnetic.

questions.prompt: Which molecule has a zero dipole moment?
questions.explanation: CO₂ is linear and symmetrical, so the two equal C=O bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel. H₂O is bent and NH₃ is pyramidal, so their bond dipoles do not cancel, and SO₂ is bent for the same reason.

questions.prompt: The hybridisation of the carbon atoms in ethyne (acetylene, C₂H₂) and the number of π bonds in the molecule are:
questions.explanation: Each carbon in HC≡CH forms two electron domains — one C–H bond and one C–C bond — so each is sp hybridised and the molecule is linear. The triple bond contains one σ bond and two π bonds formed by side-on overlap of the two remaining unhybridised p orbitals on each carbon.

questions.prompt: The number of electrons in the outermost shell required by the octet rule is __________.
questions.explanation: The octet rule states that atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons so that their valence shell holds eight electrons, like the nearest noble gas; hydrogen and helium are the exception, being stable with two (the duet rule).

questions.prompt: The bond angle in the water molecule is __________.
questions.explanation: Oxygen in water has four electron domains — two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. The lone pairs repel more strongly than the bonding pairs, compressing the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5° down to 104.5°, so the molecule is bent.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a coordinate (dative) bond and an ordinary covalent bond.
questions.answer: In an ordinary covalent bond each participating atom contributes one electron to the shared pair, whereas in a coordinate bond both electrons of the shared pair are donated by one atom. The formation of the ammonium ion, NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺, is the standard example: nitrogen's lone pair is donated to the proton. Once formed the bond is indistinguishable from the other three N–H bonds in NH₄⁺, being identical in length and strength.
questions.explanation: The key point for full marks is that the distinction applies only to how the pair originates: once formed, a coordinate bond is identical in length and strength to any other bond in the molecule.

questions.prompt: State Fajans' rules and explain why aluminium chloride has considerable covalent character.
questions.answer: Fajans' rules state that a compound acquires covalent character when the cation is small and highly charged, the anion is large and easily polarised, and the cation has a pseudo noble-gas configuration. Al³⁺ is small and triply charged, so it strongly distorts the electron cloud of the large Cl⁻ ion, drawing electron density towards itself. The resulting sharing rather than complete transfer gives AlCl₃ considerable covalent character, which is why it exists as a molecular dimer Al₂Cl₆ with a low melting point rather than as a typical ionic lattice.
questions.explanation: Fajans' rules are the accepted explanation for covalent character in apparently ionic compounds, and aluminium chloride is the standard example because of the small, highly charged Al3+ ion.

questions.prompt: Using VSEPR, predict the geometry and bond angle of sulphur hexafluoride SF₆ and explain the arrangement of its electron pairs.
questions.answer: The central sulphur atom has six valence electrons, each forming a single bond with a fluorine atom, so there are six bonding domains and no lone pairs. Six electron domains minimise their mutual repulsion by adopting an octahedral arrangement, giving bond angles of 90° between adjacent F–S–F bonds and 180° between opposite ones. The molecule is therefore octahedral and, because all six positions are equivalent, perfectly symmetrical with a zero dipole moment. Sulphur expands its octet here because it uses its vacant 3d orbitals to accommodate more than eight electrons, giving sp³d² hybridisation built from one s, three p and two d orbitals.
questions.explanation: VSEPR answers must count the domains first and then name the molecular shape: six bonding pairs and no lone pairs give a regular octahedron with all angles equal.

questions.prompt: Compare the boiling points of water, hydrogen sulphide and hydrogen fluoride in the light of their structures, and explain the anomalous trend within group 16 and group 17.
questions.answer: Water boils at 100 °C although it is the lightest hydride of group 16; hydrogen sulphide, heavier and more polarizable, boils at −60 °C. The explanation is that O–H bonds in water are so polar that each molecule forms up to four intermolecular hydrogen bonds, creating a cohesive network that must be extensively broken before the liquid can boil. H₂S has only ordinary dipole-dipole and dispersion forces because sulphur is not electronegative enough to support hydrogen bonding, so despite its greater mass it boils far lower. The same pattern holds in group 17: HF boils at 19.5 °C while HCl, three times heavier, boils at −85 °C, because HF molecules hydrogen-bond into (HF)ₙ chains. Within each group, therefore, the second member breaks the expected mass-based trend, and the anomaly disappears in H₂O, HF and NH₃ only because hydrogen bonding requires the small, highly electronegative atoms N, O and F.
questions.explanation: Boiling-point comparisons must separate intermolecular forces from molecular mass; hydrogen bonding is the only force that explains why the lightest member of each group boils highest.
